text: Kahneman shows us how System 1 isn’t just quick—it’s our default survival mechanism. It makes instant judgments, spots threats, drives cars for us when we daydream or get distracted, reads facial expressions, and fills in missing pieces of perception. It’s powerful and high speed but low depth. System 2, on the other hand, Kahneman likens to a board of directors. Slow to convene, expensive to operate, but necessary for tough calls. It doesn’t like to be bothered. Most of the time, it isn’t. System 1 is operating at a speed your conscious brain could barely comprehend. By orders of magnitude, unconscious processing vastly exceeds conscious processing in the human brain. There is a part of our brain that is always running beneath the surface—a subconscious prediction engine. It is constantly scanning our environment for familiar patterns and potential hostile risk patterns, comparing incoming signals to a developed set of expectations. We don’t even realize it’s happening until something unexpected breaks the pattern. You will recall here from Dehaene that we are born with this model already intact. Is That a Face? To this, the middle layers would frequently stop the ascension through to even higher layers, sending the information back down, as if saying, “No, that’s just a coconut.” This layered dance of perception and interpretation sets the stage for one of the brain’s most powerful learning tools: prediction error. The information is processed quickly and dismissed. But if the pattern is unfamiliar or ambiguous, the signal is escalated upward to higher cortical regions for additional scrutiny and more nuanced interpretation. For prediction model updating. For learning. For building our model of the world. Prediction Error: A Shared Language of Learning In neuroscience, this is known as predictive coding. It suggests that the brain is constantly making forecasts about incoming sensory information based on prior experience (memory). When those predictions match our perceptions of reality, the brain operates efficiently with minimal adjustment. But when there’s a mismatch—a prediction error—the brain doesn’t treat it as failure. It treats it as a signal for learning. This prediction-error cycle has become central to how AI systems learn and adapt. In supervised learning, for example, AI systems compare predictions to desired outcomes, use the difference as an error signal, and adjust accordingly. While the details differ, the underlying idea of learning through feedback and correction provides a useful bridge between how biological and artificial systems improve over time. The Gold Standard Understanding how this early learning unfolds prepares us to see how its core principles—prediction, feedback, and correction—became the scaffolding for modern AI. As we transition our discussion from biological into artificial intelligence and neural networks, it’s essential to hold on to this image: Even as newborn infants, our brains are optimizing observation into learning in real time. We explored how this prediction model works with spectacular energy efficiency using a series of neurological steps or layers that operate in harmony but very differently, fast and slow. Our brain’s prediction-feedback-response learning mechanism is the gold standard that makes AI work. When you hear “training an AI model,” that is a big part of what is happening. And you will recall from our earlier discussion that we didn’t exactly build AI. We gave it a learning architecture and taught it how to learn. And then it did. OceanofPDF.com CHAPTER 6 The Two AI Winters For most of the twentieth century, the dream of artificial intelligence sparkled with promise—and regularly collapsed under its own weight. The First AI Winter In the early days, researchers believed that to build an intelligent machine, all one had to do was program in the facts. If you could load a database with enough data about the world, surely intelligence would emerge. It didn’t. The first major efforts at AI were logic-based, rule-bound systems. These “expert systems” worked in narrow domains, such as diagnosing car trouble or medical conditions—so long as all the relevant information was hand-coded into the system. But the real world is messy. It’s full of nuance, contradiction, and edge cases. The failure of these early models became apparent, and expectations plummeted. This disappointment marked the first AI winter in the 1970s—a deep freeze in funding, credibility, and academic interest. The Second AI Winter But hope is persistent. Artificial intelligence in the 1970s and early 1980s was dominated by symbolic approaches—systems that relied on logic, search trees, and hand-coded rules to simulate intelligence. These systems achieved early success in constrained domains such as game playing and expert systems, but they struggled with ambiguity, perception, and the messy, continuous nature of real-world data. As these limitations became clearer, frustration grew. Yet an older idea quietly resurfaced. Decades earlier, in the 1950s and 1960s, pioneers such as Frank Rosenblatt had introduced the perceptron—a simplified model of a neuron that could learn to recognize patterns. But the limitations of early neural networks were sharply criticized in a 1969 book by Marvin L. Minsky and Seymour Papert, which pointed out that single-layer networks couldn’t solve even basic logical functions. 32 Then, in the mid-1980s, that story changed. A small group of researchers—including Geoffrey Hinton (we spoke about him earlier), David Rumelhart, and Ronald Williams—revived the field with a powerful updated insight: If you stacked multiple layers of simple neuron-like units and trained them using a technique called backpropagation, a training method that computes how wrong the network’s outputs are and then adjusts each layer’s connections to reduce that error, these neural networks could, in principle, learn rich internal representations of complex data.
